Trend in a count series, as a rate ratio per period

Source: R/trend.R
cnttrnd.Rd

Estimates the trend in a series of counts (arrests, admissions, incidents per year) as a rate ratio per period: 0.85 means the count falls by 15% a year. It fits a Poisson log-linear model and, when the counts vary more than a Poisson model allows, widens the interval. An offset carries the denominator when the exposure varies, so the trend is then in the rate rather than in the count.

Usage

cnttrnd(y, x = NULL, offset = NULL, conflvl = 0.95)

Arguments

y

Numeric vector of counts (non-negative whole numbers), in period order.

x

Numeric vector of periods, default NULL (the position). The rate ratio is per unit of x.

offset

Optional numeric vector of exposures, one per period – a population, a number of admissions, a number of days. Positive. The trend is then in the rate rather than in the count.

conflvl

Number in (0, 1), default 0.95: the confidence level of the rate-ratio interval.

Value

A list of class c("rmbl_count_trend", "list") with rateratio (per period), lower, upper, p_value (test of no trend), logslope (\(\beta_1\)), se (its standard error, scaled when overdispersed), fitted (fitted counts), dispersion, overdispersed (logical), n, data (list of the x and y used) and method.

Details

The model is \(\log \mu_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_t - \bar x) + \log o_t\), with \(o_t\) the offset (1 when none), fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares (at most 50 iterations). The rate ratio is \(e^{\beta_1}\), with a Wald interval \(e^{\beta_1 \pm z\, \mathrm{se}}\).

The dispersion is reported because a Poisson fit assumes it is one. It is the Pearson statistic \(\sum (y - \mu)^2/\mu\) divided by \(n - 2\). When it exceeds 1.5 the quasi-Poisson interval is returned instead: the standard error is multiplied by the square root of the dispersion and the \(t\) distribution on \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom replaces the normal, and overdispersed is set.

Missing values are dropped. Errors: negative or fractional counts; x and y of different lengths; infinite x; every count zero; an offset of the wrong length or not positive; fewer than three periods; a conflvl outside (0, 1). When the counts are zero at one end of the series only (c(0, 0, 5)) the likelihood rises without bound and there is no finite trend: a warning says so, the rate ratio is Inf (or 0) and the interval and p-value are NA. There is a plot() method for the result.

References

Bilder, C. R. and Loughin, T. M. Analysis of Categorical Data with R, 2nd edn. Chapman and Hall/CRC, on the quasi-likelihood treatment of an overdispersed Poisson fit: the variance is scaled by an estimated dispersion, which widens the interval while leaving the point estimate alone. That is the behaviour reported here through dispersion and overdispersed.

See also

trndtst, ratechg.

Examples

# A count falling by about 15% a year.
set.seed(3)
y <- stats::rpois(8, lambda = 200 * 0.85^(0:7))
fit <- cnttrnd(y)
round(fit$rateratio, 3)
#> [1] 0.869
c(fit$lower, fit$upper)
#> [1] 0.8444785 0.8942357

# With a varying denominator the trend is in the rate.
cnttrnd(c(20, 25, 30), offset = c(1000, 1500, 2500))$rateratio
#> [1] 0.7708656

# Counts that swing far more than Poisson noise get the wider interval.
wild <- cnttrnd(c(10, 50, 5, 60, 8, 70))
wild$dispersion
#> [1] 26.27417
wild$method
#> [1] "quasi-Poisson (dispersion above 1.5)"

try(cnttrnd(c(1.5, 2, 3)))
#> Error : `y` must be non-negative whole numbers
